title: Garuda and the nectar
hookLine: Garuda steals the nectar of the gods to buy his mother's freedom, and never tastes a drop
carry: seva: serve without taking a sip
tomorrow: why would a king hang a dead snake on a silent sage?
last: THE NAGAS ARE HONORED, NOT HATED.

cards: An egg cracks open and something blazing comes out, so bright the gods take it for fire. It's Garuda, Vinata's son, a bird of enormous strength.

He grows up to find his mother a slave to her sister, made to carry the snakes wherever they want to go. So he asks the snakes the obvious question: what would it take to set her free? They name a price nobody could pay.
Bring us the amrita, the nectar of immortality, which the gods keep for themselves.

teach.b: So Garuda goes to get it. He fights past the gods and a spinning wheel of blades, and takes the amrita. The first surprise: he doesn't drink it.
He could make himself immortal on the spot, and he carries it away untouched, because it's for his mother's freedom.
Vishnu is so pleased that he grants Garuda boons: a place on Vishnu's banner, and immortality without a drop of the nectar. Garuda offers a boon in return, and Vishnu asks him to be his mount.
Then Indra, king of the gods, asks for the nectar back. Garuda makes him an offer: I've promised it to the snakes, and I'll let no one drink it. But wherever I set it down, you may take it up.
Garuda sets the nectar down for the snakes on a bed of kusha grass. My mother is free, he says. Go and bathe before you drink.
While they bathe, Indra takes the amrita back to heaven, as agreed. The snakes lick the empty grass, and its sharp blades split their tongues.
That, the story says, is why snakes have forked tongues, and why kusha grass is held holy. Now the teaching Hindus keep from it.
The one who held immortality in his claws and didn't take a sip is the one Vishnu chose to carry him.

teach.h: SEVA: SERVE WITHOUT TAKING A SIP.
teach.b: That's seva, service, at the heart of bhakti: you carry what's precious, and you don't help yourself along the way. In many Vishnu temples, Garuda stands before the shrine with folded hands, facing his Lord.

how: In many Vishnu temples, especially in South India, an image of Garuda stands facing the shrine with folded hands, as Vishnu's mount and model servant. Kusha (darbha) grass is used in many Hindu rites, and some families retell Garuda's story to children as a story of loyalty to a mother.

games.q: Garuda and the nectar — tap the pairs.

s: Garuda drank the amrita before handing it over
he carried it away untouched; it was for his mother's freedom.
Garuda freed Vinata by paying the snakes' price
he set the nectar before them, and his mother was free.
Indra took it back while they bathed; they only licked the grass.

games.q: you help in the temple kitchen, and trays of sweets pass through your hands all morning before the puja. by Garuda's story, what's seva here?
o: serve them out, and taste only once the offering is made and everyone has been fed.
take one now; a taste is fine, the work is the point.
skip the kitchen and just donate; it's the same thing.
games.why: Garuda carried the gods' nectar and never took a sip, and Vishnu chose him to carry him. in Hindu temples, food is offered to God before anyone tastes it.

practice: Garuda carried the gods' own nectar and never took a sip. Pick one small act of seva you can do today for someone at home: a dish, an errand, a cup of tea made the way they like it. Do it without mentioning it.
If you pray, offer it quietly to God as you do it; if not, just notice the pull to take a little credit, and let it pass.

wordCard.voice: Adi Parva. The opening book, where Garuda steals the gods' nectar to free his mother, and never tastes it.

orig.note: Sanskrit amṛta, the nectar of immortality: Garuda's price for his mother's freedom.

carryVoice: Carry this: seva, serve without taking a sip. His mother walks free. Tomorrow: why would a king hang a dead snake on a silent sage? See you tomorrow.
